Regarding the phrase "because it serves as a cause for that which is contradictory": for example, when one establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) of permanence, impermanence is contradictory to that thesis of permanence.
Since the reason (*hetu*) of being a product (*kṛtakatva*) serves as a cause for the property of impermanence, it is called a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*).
Here, "contradiction" is the effect and the "reason" is what obtains the name of the effect; thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative).

The objection that a "contradictory reason" (*viruddha-hetu*) cannot be established merely by violating the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the example (*udāharaṇa*) is addressed here as follows: the name "contradictory" is applied to the reason based on its own nature;

it is not the case that the reason causes the thesis to be reversed and thereby receives the name "contradictory. Rather, it is called a "contradictory reason" simply because it serves as a reason that is contradictory to that [thesis].

Once this is understood, there is no longer the fault of having to establish a separate category for a "contradictory reason" based on the violation of the thesis or the example. This is the intended meaning.
This is precisely because the reason (*hetu*) does not contradict the thesis (*pakṣa*); it receives the designation "contradictory" (*viruddha*) only from the perspective of a contradictory property.
If this were the case, why would it be said that the previously stated reason—without being altered—can cause the proponent’s thesis to become contradictory?

Furthermore, according to this statement, one could still raise the objection that the thesis contradicts the reason, thereby creating a formal difficulty (*dūṣaṇa*). Why, then, is it said that there is none? This explanation is merely provisional.
Based on the reason (*hetu*), one obtains its name; it belongs to oneself and is definitively contradictory.

Furthermore, this interpretation—that the actual attainment of the name is itself a type of "one-sided" (*ekāṃśika*)—is understood through the following question and answer as being an instance of the fallacy of "one-sidedness. Question:

Since both the "one-sided contradiction" (*ekāṃśika-viruddha*) and the "fourfold contradiction" (*caturvidha-viruddha*) cause the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be overturned by means of the reason, they are given the same name.
What is the difference between the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) and the counter-balanced contradictory reason (*pratibādhita-viruddha*)? The answer is:

the counter-balanced contradictory reason necessarily requires the alteration of the original reason, whereas these four types of contradictory reasons do not require such alteration; thus, there is a distinction between the two.

The meaning of the statement "as it is with non-contradiction, so it is with contradiction" is as follows: when one establishes sound as produced and yet claims it is eternal, this is called "non-contradiction" from the perspective of others who have established it as such.
If a contradiction were established, then even the thesis of impermanence would likewise not be contradictory;
therefore, it is said that "as it is with non-contradiction, so it is with contradiction."
Regarding the phrase "because the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) lacks a definite non-existence," the intended meaning is as follows:

when the probans (*hetu*) of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is used to prove "permanence," it cannot be called a property to be proven that lacks a definite non-existence, because there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as space (*ākāśa*) upon which such a definite non-existence could be established.

Regarding the phrase "because it is stated by him," this refers to the *Nyāyamukha*. Its general meaning is that one wishes to clearly understand that [the reason] is not a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacy because it contradicts the thesis (*pakṣa*);

rather, it is named "contradictory" because it contradicts the intended property (*dharma*). Question: Although the *Nyāyamukha* is cited, how do we know that this specifically refers to the reason (*hetu*) not contradicting the thesis?

Answer: The *Nyāyamukha* states: "If a factor (*dharma*) can establish something contradictory to what is to be established (*sādhyaviparīta*), it is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhahetu*), and is thus called a 'pseudo-reason' (*hetvābhāsa*)."
Just as with the "contradiction of the non-contradictory" (*aviruddha-viruddha*), it is clearly understood that this is not a case of the reason contradicting the thesis. Question:

Regarding the four types of contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*) termed "pseudo-reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*), with respect to what are they pseudo? Answer: They are termed "pseudo" with respect to the original proponent who put forward the contradiction;
they are not termed "pseudo" with respect to the person who points out the fault. With respect to the one pointing out the fault, these are in fact genuine [capable] reasons.
[This] refutes [the opponent].

This school’s doctrine of the Dharma is the system of this *Hetuvidyā* treatise. Question: Why does the adversary lack *hetuvidyā*, and why do you not propose a concise refutation until now, only to speak of this school at this point?
Answer: Here, we are precisely clarifying that among the four types of contradiction (*viruddha*), there is the contradiction of essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddha*).
Because there is a distinction, it is only in this context that this particular tenet is taught; since there is this difference, one should not find fault with it.
Although this is indeed the same as what preceded it, the teaching is slightly different and the meaning is also distinct.

To say that the teaching is different means that the two treatises, the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, differ, which is termed a difference in teaching (*śāsana-bheda*). This is stated from the perspective of the specific distinctions in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), while the other refers to—
The former presentation and the subsequent explanation are not fixed, as the names and meanings differ.

Third, regarding the statement that "the assertions and the limits all have distinctions," this third pair of statements, within its presentation, subsumes the previous two gates according to what is appropriate.
If one relies on the manifestation of the meaning, it only subsumes the second [gate]. Why does it not subsume [the others]?
The initial [category] was restricted to the general response to the "heretical" (yā) [position];

since within that general [response] there were already distinctions such as pervasive and non-pervasive, why would the third [category] exclude the "explicit statement" (vacana) and claim that everything else is a distinction?

If it were the case that the explicit statement itself constitutes a distinction, then how could one further speak of "intended distinctions" (abhiprāya-viśeṣa)? Since this [intended distinction] is not included in the first category, [the third category is necessary].

Although this is not as comprehensive as the summary [of the categories], the meaning of the phrase "from that first statement" is as follows: it refers to the contradiction with inference (*anumāna-viruddha*) and the counter-balanced contradiction (*pratibādhita-viruddha*), both of which were previously stated as contradictions regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*).
This is because they are explained from among those four types of contradiction starting with the first contradiction; hence, it says "from that first statement."
He also asked: "For what reason, among the four types of contradiction (*viruddha*), is the contradiction regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the thesis stated first? He replied:
"It is that which is directly contested. Since the other contradictions are determined through inference (*anumāna*) based upon that direct contestation, it is stated at the beginning."

"If it were not so, there would necessarily be no [such] factors as 'dharma' and so forth"—the meaning of this is that among the four types of contradiction, in the first case one must change the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), while in the latter three cases one may either change or not change the example, or leave it as it is.
If one says that a single reason (*hetu*) contradicts two theses (*pakṣa*), then the three theses must necessarily have their examples changed;
however, according to the text of the treatise, in the first case the example is changed, but in the latter three cases it is not changed.

Regarding the statement that "the first [example] is permitted to be modified while the latter three are not," this explains that there must be no contradiction with the two-fold combination or the three-fold combination within the unmodified example.

Is it not the case that the meaning of "contradiction regarding the specific characteristic of the subject" (*dharmisvarūpaviruddha*) implies that even if an opponent were to raise an objection, could there possibly be no such subject?

Is it a contradiction of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? It is not that there is a contradiction of the specific characteristic of the subject (*dharmin*); rather, it is a fault regarding the specific characteristic of the property (*dharma*).
[The opponent] replies: "It cannot be so, as stated in the commentary.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "impermanence does not reach the locus of the substratum," etc., the adversary cites the two [reasons] for the subject "sound is impermanent" as being the locus of the property (*dharmin*).
To establish "being produced" as the reason also commits the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) in part.
Among all those who formulate such pseudo-reasons, this specific type of pseudo-reason is not observed within their formulations.
Regarding the phrase "that which can be heard upon the permanent sound," the intended meaning is as follows: the specific quality (viśeṣa) upon the permanent sound is that the sound is audible;
the absence of self (anātman) within the sound is not itself an audible quality.

Alternatively, it may mean that while the sound can be expressed through conventional designations, it is audible when conditions coincide and inaudible when they do not; this too is a specific quality of the sound.
Regarding the phrase "acting as that causal condition or not acting as that causal condition" (*tad-pratyayatā-tad-apratyayatā*) upon impermanence:

the intended meaning is that while the sound of impermanence serves as the objective sphere (*ālambana*) for the mind that perceives the impermanence of that sound, it does not act as the causal nature (*svabhāva*) for that mind.
That it does not act as its causal nature is also a sense of differentiation within the context of impermanence; therefore, it is said to "act as that."
The nature of a condition is not that which is the nature of its opposite condition. To state the general meaning:

a "reason contradictory by way of distinction" (viśeṣaviruddha-hetu) is so called because it is a reason accepted by the proponent according to the specific requirements of the case, yet it contradicts that [opposite].

It does not mean that every distinct phenomenon serves as a cause for everything; if something were to serve as a cause for all things, there would be no such thing as a contradictory cause, nor would there be any non-contradictory cause.

There is a similar example (*sapakṣa*). Question: Although previously you cited "permanent" and "impermanent," and "audible" and "inaudible" as the nature of those conditions (*pratyaya*) to distinguish their differences, it remains unknown whether these differences pertain to the subject (*dharmin*) or to the attributes (*dharma*) thereof. Answer:
"Audible" and "inaudible" are differences of the subject; "acting as a condition" and "not acting as a condition" are differences of the attributes.
Regarding the statement "the meaning explained herein," this intends to explain the purpose for which the eyes and so forth are established as being for the sake of another within this text.

As for the phrase "this reason, such as the capacity to establish the eyes and so forth," the intended meaning here is that the Sāṃkhya school falsely posits the reason of "composite nature" (*saṃghātatva*) to establish that the eyes and so forth must necessarily exist for the sake of another.
In view of what intention is this established as the true purpose of being for the sake of another? This is the point of the treatise.
The statement "this reason is like that which establishes the eye and so forth" uses "like" (*yathā*) to indicate a locus (*sthāna*).

When the treatise says "in this way it can also establish the eye and so forth," it refers to the fact that the reason— the nature of being an accumulation— is contradictory to the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
If one considers the real self (*puruṣa*) to be superior because it is that which thinks, the intention here is as follows:

if there were no conscious self, objects such as bedding would not undergo transformation through thought; since it is only after thinking occurs that they transform, the real self is superior to the bedding and such.
Furthermore, regarding the necessity of a place for rest, the provisional self is superior to the bedding. Now, this is based on the provisional self that experiences the use of others.
Because it possesses these superior qualities, it is difficult [to refute].

Regarding the claim that there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) within a common inference (*sādhāraṇānumāna*): according to the inference established by the Sāṃkhya teachers, this is indeed a common one.

The response states: "In reality, because the self (*ātman*) is inferior, there is simply no similar instance. As for an inference belonging to another [school], if it were [based on] the Great [Principle] (*mahat*),...

If you maintain that the sense organs, such as the eye, are substantially existent but their functions are inferior, then there is no fault in asserting that they are not obstructed by anything else through inference.
As for the masters of the Western Regions who hold that [atoms] do not aggregate for the sake of another, this describes those in the West who were unskilled in *hetuvidyā* (logic).

This means that while the opponent’s statement claims that the eyes and so forth exist solely for the sake of others who are not aggregates, and that beds and seats serve both purposes (for oneself and for others), [the proponent] directly states the fault:
"The eyes and so forth should exist for the sake of others who are aggregates," and so on; thus, this now commits the fallacy of *pratijñā-virodha* (contradiction with one's own thesis).
Furthermore, regarding the explanation by the masters of the Western Regions as previously analyzed:

the intention here is to state that while the preceding passage cited the objection that the eyes and so forth serve only for the purpose of an accumulation, one should now also allow that the eyes and so forth serve for the purpose of that which is not an accumulation;

thus, there is no fault of inconsistency. Nevertheless, even with this determination, one still loses the fundamental intent of the opponent's school. [The author] extensively expounds the principles and cites evidence.
This can be understood from the text.
One should not give rise to divergent interpretations regarding this; it is the conclusion of the preceding section, or alternatively, it may be read as belonging to the following section.

As for the statement that the eyes and so forth function only as actual things for the enjoyment of others, while bedding and furniture function only as provisional things—this is not [the view of] the Westerners (i.e., the Vaibhāṣikas).
The Master’s explanation is as follows: this is also the teaching of Master Gui; therefore, one should not give rise to divergent views regarding this conclusion.
Consequently, if one explains it according to this commentary, the difficulty concerning superiority and inferiority will be without fault.
Furthermore, regarding the fault of the distinction between dharmas (*dharma-viśeṣa*) herein, the meaning is as follows:

the *Seventy Verses on Ultimate Truth* also interrogates that Sāṃkhya teacher because he commits the fault of distinction by establishing this single category; thus, it is said to be "the distinction between dharmas herein."

Regarding the passage, "After many kalpas, the Brahmins and others asked," based on the statement of these outsiders that the kalpa of formation has not yet ended, what kind of kalpa is meant by "many kalpas"?
Answer: It does not mean "many" in the sense of the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness;

rather, it is called "many" based on the kalpas measured by days, months, and years. Furthermore, even if one were to posit that [the world] had passed through two kalpas of abiding, there would be no fault in that.
"Thirty trillion *pañca-śikha* [deities] are also called 'many eons' (*bahu-kalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "above these three, up to the essence, are constantly numerous," this describes the categories of identity and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) according to that school;

in total, there are two kinds: first, general identity and difference, and second, specific identity and difference. Within general identity and difference, there are further two types: first, the general...

Among the three—generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya)—the nine substances share the common name "substance," and they are likewise named by their qualities and activities;

thus, these three types of phenomena are collectively termed "generalities" (sāmānya). Their mutual distinctions are termed "particularities" (viśeṣa). Within the second category, "distinct generalities and particularities" (bhinna-sāmānya-viśeṣa), there are also two:

first, distinct generalities, and second, distinct particularities. The nine substances share the commonality of being "substances," which is designated as their "generality"; because this very distinction [of being substances] constitutes their generality, it is called "distinct generality."
The statement regarding the distinction between the same [substance] and its qualities and activities is likewise. Earth is distinct from water and so forth; this is called "distinctness.

Qualities and activities are also to be understood according to this principle. Therefore, the commentary states: "Upon each of these three, there is respectively one universal generality (sāmānya) and particularity (viśeṣa);
accordingly, each possesses its own particular generality and particularity, just as was previously analyzed and concluded."

Regarding the wording of that commentary: "Among these three [categories], according to their respective specific types, there are further general and specific commonalities and differences"—this means that within the three [categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, pointing to any single dharma is termed a "specific type.

Within those such as earth-substance (*pṛthivī-dravya*) and so forth, there is likewise the sense of general and specific commonalities and differences; for instance, among earth-substances, two substances, many substances, and so forth, are collectively termed "substance."
Parents are not their children, and children are not their grandchildren; each is distinct from the others. This is termed "the general and the particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Interpreting it according to this principle, there may further be cases of the general and the particular, which refer back to the aforementioned "general and particular" as either identical or different. These are summarized into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for analysis:
first, that which is only general and not particular—namely, substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*); second, that which is only particular and not... [text fragmentary].
In general, it is said that among the real entities such as earth and so forth, when multiple atoms and the like exist together, they are both "general" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*).

That is to say, the nine real entities are "general" because they share the common nature of being real entities (*dravyapada*); they are "particular" because the nine combined are not identical. The rest should be understood accordingly.
The meaning of the phrase "the capacity to be non-non-existent" (*aśūnyatva*) is as follows: it merely implies that what is expressed by the words is not non-existent;

thus, it is said that there is a name which has the capacity to be non-non-existent. This establishes the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). However, if one were to explicitly state that "there is a great name" (*mahān nāma*) which truly possesses the capacity to be non-non-existent upon substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), or activity (*karman*), then one would commit the fallacy of the unestablished locus of the property to be proven (*asiddha-viśeṣya*).
Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) would likewise commit the fallacy of being unestablished with respect to at least one of its substrata (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus it is said.
Because they are few, they are briefly stated as "due to the transgression of any one [of them].
Regarding the phrase "the four fundamental atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows: the four fundamental atoms are termed "empty space" (*ākāśa*).

Although the five entities—space and the others—are each individually singular, despite their differences in quantity, none of them arise from a real cause; therefore, they are all designated as "non-existent."
Indeed, regarding the two realities of the subtle name "fruit": the subtle name "seed" is the capacity to produce father and mother, which constitutes that which is possessed;
because the subtle name "seed" possesses this, it establishes its name as having two realities.
Regarding the phrase "the triad of three combined for production, and the septet of seven combined," the intended meaning here is as follows:

the descendants are subtle while the parents are generally impermanent; they serve as the progenitors for the descendants and so forth. Even down to the great earth that can produce [all things], within that which is produced there is no original father or mother;

once the descendant has come into being, it is entirely impermanent. Within the producer, there is the permanent, the impermanent, the cause, the condition, the primary factor, and the auxiliary factors. The permanent [element] exists therein.
To say that [the former] assists impermanence while [the latter] is the primary [meaning], though such an interpretation exists, it is not yet settled.
For instance, when the Buddha’s teachings speak of "form" (rūpa) being "outflowing" (sāsrava) and so forth, this is cited as an illustration: the essence of affliction is termed "outflow" (āsrava);

because wholesome dharmas can possess [afflictions], they are called "with outflow" (sāsrava). Because great conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) can possess reality, they are "possessions" (svabhāva); because they can possess existence, they are "existent" (bhava).

When all these are combined and referred to as "existence" (*sat*) or "real existence," the expression "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) is likewise applied. That which possesses the capacity to have and that which is possessed have distinct natures;

this is what is called "with outflows. As for the term "possessing form" (*rūpin*), it is like there being a single reality that belongs to the substance of attachment itself, rather than having a separate capacity to possess, just as sound exists within space. It is likewise not the case that there is something existing apart from space.
However, regarding the statement that "the term 'possessing' refers to a single real entity," one asks the Vaiśeṣika teacher: what is the intention behind citing such an example?
The answer is: the thesis statement "there is existence" is like the [term] "with outflows" (*sāsrava*); this is a comprehensive expression.

As for the mention of "possessing a single real entity" and so forth within the reason (*hetu*), since a reason must be common [to both the similar and dissimilar classes], the phrase "possessing form" (*rūpin*) is cited as an illustration of the reason.
There is no violation of even a single [rule].
If it is said that "existence" and "non-existence" are both indeterminate (*aniścita*) because they apply to both sides, the intention is this:

generally, when a reason is indeterminate for both sides, neither the proponent nor the opponent admits its occurrence upon the subject (*dharmin*) presented in the thesis. Now, in the formulation of the thesis, one speaks of "the nature of existence."
This is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*). This existence has the capacity to possess the three—substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)—which are precisely these three:

substance, quality, and action. This capacity is not non-existent; it is admitted by both the proponent and the opponent. Furthermore, the statement of the reason (*hetu*) is that "it does not have real [substance, etc.].

The term "non-real" applies to the category of the composite (*sāmānyasamavāya*). This is not admitted by either the proponent or the opponent. [The proponent] maintains that there is the capacity for those [substances, etc. to exist within that composite category.

If there were no real entity, this would constitute the fallacy of "non-establishment of both parts" (ubhayāsiddha) due to the violation of [the requirement that] both [probandum and reason] must be established;
for a real cause does not apply to a subject (pakṣa) that lacks a real entity, nor does it function upon a nature that is non-existent.

Regarding the statement, "Because reality and so forth can have a superior [state], there is no such thing as non-reality," this explains why the reason (hetu) commits the fallacy of being unestablished for both parties.
As for the example also committing the fallacy of the unestablished probans (sādhanābhāsa), it refers to using "because there is non-reality" as the reason; its [corresponding] similar instance...

If the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) cannot possess the absence of reality in the phrase "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), then by this same principle, it is also a case where one part of the probans (*sādhanāṅga*) is unestablished in the example.
Question: What is meant by "one part"? Answer: Both the similar (*sādharmya*) and dissimilar examples must be able to possess the absence of reality within the phrase "in the middle of the real.
Since they both lack the absence of reality in the phrase "conjunction," the probans is unestablished in one part of the example.

The reason (*hetu*) is also not pervasive (*avyāpin*), as stated in the Commentary (*vṛtti*): "It appears at first glance that [the reason] can only apply to the absence of 'real' within the category of 'real' (*sat-padārtha*).
This explains why the reason is not pervasive; that is to say, it cannot apply to cases such as "two reals" or "many reals" within the category of "real.
Thus, the reason is said to be non-pervasive, or perhaps may be non-pervasive, because there exists the reason of "non-reality" (*asat-hetu*).
If the existence [of the reason] is not pervasive across all instances of existence, then one does not admit that existence resides in the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

Since the opponent holds that existence is not a real entity but rather a non-existent [quality], existence does not reside in conjunction; therefore, the reason is also not pervasive. Alternatively, it may be that [the reason] is not pervasive within the category of conjunction itself.

Question: Regarding the statement that "existence" (*sattā*), "the property of existence" (*sattva*), and "one real cause" (*eka-vastu-hetu*) are [the probans], what is the intended meaning of this question?

It means that while the term "existence" is established in reference to the fundamental [category] as "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*), when one cites "one real cause" as the reason, this refers to an existence that is commonly admitted to be non-void.

Since this [reason] does not at all correspond to the "property of existence" (*dharmin*) of the thesis (*pakṣa*), why is it not a "fallacy common to both parties" (*ubhaya-sapakṣa-doṣa*)? Answer: It is merely stated that...
The response, "Briefly stated, the reason for existence depends upon that," means there is no fault; for the objector simply took "Great Existence" as the subject of inquiry.

When one investigates it, the qualities and activities are not distinguished [as being merely Great Existence], so there is no need for a single word [to define it]. This implies that within reality, there are distinctions such as the real, the unreal, the manifold, and the singular.

Since there are many faults [if one were to posit existence] and because there is a need for distinction, one merely states "there is one real entity" (*eka-dravya*); this immediately excludes all such faults.
Since among qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*) there is no such distinction that could be singled out, it is unnecessary to attach the term "one" to qualities, activities, and so forth;
therefore, the commentary states: "Since qualities and activities lack such distinction, the word 'one' is not required."

Regarding the statement, "Restating that thesis and reiterating the critique," the meaning is as follows: "reiterating" (*liàng*) refers to restating the fault; "only one" (*yī*) refers to the single point of departure;
and "containing" (*hán*) refers to the composition of the words. Thus, it is called "restating the critique."
Regarding the phrase "because both are determined," the intended meaning is as follows: since there will be a real entity (*vastu*), the reason (*hetu*) establishes the original thesis (*pakṣa*).
If one were to depart from the existence of a real essence, then by means of this very reason, one would also establish for the opponent that [the entity] is not non-existent.

Thus, while these two determinations appear to be established determinations in relation to the original proponent, they are truly refuting determinations in relation to the one who points out the fault; they are not [determinations] shared by both the proponent and the opponent.
"True determination" refers to the "determination of both. Question: According to the four types of contradiction, all of them are equally absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*);
why then does the treatise state that the latter two are "determined for both," while it does not say so for the former two?
What is the intended meaning? Answer: In truth, all four should be included; however, because the teaching is presented concisely, one should not hold this against it.

Furthermore, in all theses, there would be no similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Others raise this objection: "Since sound and a jar are distinct, a jar should not be able to serve as a similar instance for sound.

Now, we counter-objection: if you allow that which is not sound to be a similar instance for the thesis [of sound], it would not only contradict the treatise, but all theses would likewise lack similar instances.
Moreover, some original texts state that there are no dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) at all.

The [opponent’s] intention is this: if even distinct phenomena—such as the audible nature of sound and the visible nature of a jar being burned—can still be designated as "similar instances" (sapakṣa), then all distinct phenomena would necessarily become similar instances.
If everything were taken as a similar instance, there would be no dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) whatsoever for any thesis (pakṣa).
Why? Because distinct phenomena would have become identical to the similar instances.

If it were not so, there would be the fault that all "distinguished objects" (*viśeṣya*) would be unestablished; this is because it would contradict one's own tenet. The meaning of this is as follows:

if one does not raise an objection against what is intended by the proponent—that there exists a "non-existence" (*abhāva*) that is not a "great generality" (*mahāsāmānya*)—then why is it not itself established?

It is merely that all such "distinguished objects" would be unestablished, which constitutes this fault; furthermore, it would also contradict the ten propositions of the *Pañcakrama* (Five Stages). Question: In what way does it contradict them?
The Proponent replies: If there were no distinct object of negation, [the thesis] would not be established; it is simply that what is combined is not a non-existent thing.
Now, you further challenge this by saying, "Existence is not existence"—who else would be willing to commit such a contradiction with their own tenet?
Question: Regarding the objection that the "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya) as a real entity is not established for either [of the two parties], the intent is this:

if one were to state the true refutation, "The Great Universal is not a Great Universal," this statement would commit the fallacy of *svarūpāsiddhi* (unestablished in its own nature) regarding both the subject (*viśeṣya*) and the locus (*āśraya*), and it would also commit the fallacy of *pratijñāvirodha* (contradiction with one's own tenet).
Furthermore, the fallacy of being unestablished for either party applies to both the tenet and the reason; it should also apply to the tenet itself.

If that which exists were not to exist, it would constitute a direct transgression consistent with the fundamental teacher’s [teaching] and would not deviate from reality; yet this is not the case.

Regarding the claim that "the words are identical but the meanings differ, and thus there are no faults," this is the fundamental intention of the Vaiśeṣika school:

they establish two types of existence—existence as expressed by the word "exists" (*asti*) and existence as the non-existence of non-existence (*anastitva*). That which is posited within the sense of "existence" is precisely the Great Existence (*mahāsattā*).

Therefore, it is said that the words are identical while the meanings differ. As for the inclusion of the intended meaning according to the verbal expression, this is merely the fault of contradicting its own specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*), not a fault of differentiation (*viśeṣa*).

The reason (*hetu*) is also devoid of the aforementioned faults, such as those concerning the locus (*āśraya*) and so forth. If one were to state that "existence" exists when asserting it to another, one would challenge the other's statement;
yet if one were to say that existence is not existent, one would commit the fault of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*).

Regarding the statement that "those with such a nature are certainly not produced," etc.: because their essence is eternally abiding and does not arise from anything produced, they are said to be "unproduced and eternal."
That which lacks virtue is not the basis for the phrase "great virtue"; therefore, it is called "lack of virtue. Although it functions as the nature of virtue, it does not serve as its basis;
rather, it is the virtue of the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
"Without movement" means that it does not share the same category as karma, for while karma involves movement, this is said to be without movement.
"Without subtle parts" means that its essence is solely one; unlike the case where the essence of identity and difference consists of many, this is said to be without subtle parts.
"Is likewise" means that it, too, was not produced by prior causes.
Regarding "that which is conjoined," the intention is to cite the object of conjunction to demonstrate that the agent of conjunction does not exist.
As for "one" being a common designation for the conditions and causes, the meaning is that because the three—substance, quality, and activity—collectively possess oneness, they are termed "one."

There are those who hold that this serves as the cause for giving rise to expressions with identical denotations and cognitions with identical objects; this is like the "homogeneous character" (*sabhāgatā*) established in the Hīnayāna.

As for those who maintain that there are distinct expressions and cognitions regarding the nature of the object, the intention here is as follows: both the "Great Universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) and "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) can serve as objects that give rise to denotative expressions and cognitions.

However, while one [the Great Universal] can give rise to a denotative expression directed toward itself, the other [particularity] gives rise only to a denotative expression directed toward the homogeneous character.
Because their nature is the same, it is said that they "possess an object" (*sālambana*); yet, in terms of their verbal expression, they are distinct.

Therefore, when it is said here that [the definition] does not include mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it means that what is called "possessing an object" does not refer solely to the mind and mental factors that act as the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*).
Rather, it takes the objective entity itself (*viṣaya-vastu*) as being "possessing an object," because it serves as the object for the subject of cognition.
Because there are other conditions, it is named "having an object" (*sālambana*) by way of its fruit.

As for the statement that it is not "great existence" (*mahāsattā*) because it lacks the nature of being an objective cause capable of being an object of cognition, the intended meaning is as follows:

although the "commonality and difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is like "great existence" in that it can serve as an object to draw forth a cognizing subject, within the "substance" (*dravya*) residing upon this commonality and difference, there exists a single real cause.

To say "it exists" does not mean that there is a "great existence" (mahāsattā). If one were to speak of a "great existence," it would entail fallacies such as the inability to distinguish it from other forms of existence.

Although the wording in the treatise is brief, the meaning is rigorous and definitive; the intended sense is that, according to the logic, one ought to state that it is the "causal nature of great existence.
Since this would involve the aforementioned fallacy, the treatise has omitted it.
Question: Regarding the statement by the proponents of phonetics (*śabdavādin*) that "sound should not be sound," etc., what is the intended meaning here?

It is said that when the Buddha-dharma posits the impermanence of sound in opposition to them, the Buddha-dharma and the proponents of phonetics fall into the fallacy of "contradiction regarding the specific characteristics of the subject" (*dharmisvarūpaviruddha*).

This is because within the Buddha-dharma, sound is also admitted to have the nature of being an object of the auditory faculty (*śrotrālambanatva*), as well as being produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; thus, it serves as a parallel case.
